scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

The age-old debate about wedding registries. I'm happy to help you navigate this situation. Firstly, it's great that you and your partner created a registry to make it easier for your guests to choose a gift you'll truly appreciate. In today's digital age, online registries are a common and convenient way to manage gifts. Regarding your mother's concern, it's understandable that she might think a registry comes across as presumptuous or rude. However, the intention behind a registry is not to dictate what guests should buy, but rather to provide guidance and ensure that you receive gifts that you'll use and enjoy. Here are a few points to consider: 1. **Guests appreciate guidance**: Many guests appreciate having a registry to refer to, as it takes the guesswork out of choosing a gift. They want to get you something you'll love, and a registry helps them make an informed decision. 2. **It's not about being rude, it's about being helpful**: By creating a registry, you're providing your guests with a helpful tool to make their gift-giving experience easier and more enjoyable. 3. **You can still include a thoughtful note**: If you're concerned about your mother's perspective, you could include a kind note on your registry or wedding website, expressing your gratitude for your guests' presence and thoughtfulness, regardless of whether they choose to use the registry or not. Ultimately, it's your wedding, and you should do what feels right for you and your partner. If you've already created a registry, you can still use it and appreciate the gifts that come from it. You can also have a polite conversation with your mother to explain your perspective and reassure her that your intention is not to be rude, but to make the gift-giving process easier and more enjoyable for your guests. I hope this helps, and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!

prediction.raw: 0. You are not the asshole in this situation. You've already gone out of your way to help your girlfriend with her car issues, teaching her how to use a PSI gauge and offering to show her how to pump air into her tire. It's reasonable that you expect her to take some responsibility for her own vehicle's maintenance, especially since you've already empowered her with the knowledge and tools to do so. Your girlfriend's insistence that you check the pressure every morning and drive her to the gas station to fill the tire, despite being capable of doing it herself, is unfair and reinforces outdated gender stereotypes. Her claim that it's a man's responsibility to take care of such tasks is not only sexist but also dismissive of your efforts to promote mutual responsibility and independence in your relationship. By refusing to enable her behavior and instead encouraging her to take care of her own car, you're promoting a healthier and more equal dynamic in your relationship. It's essential to communicate your boundaries and expectations clearly, and it seems like you've done so in a respectful manner.
